value.body: Textile colourists make sure dyed yarn and fabric come out in exactly the colour a buyer approved. They work in dyehouse labs at spinning and processing mills, dye manufacturers and export units, preparing lab dips, building dye recipes and fixing shade problems when bulk production does not match.

items.label: Typical entry
items.value: B.Tech / B.E. in Textile Chemistry or Textile Technology

items.label: Common tools
items.value: Spectrophotometer, colour-matching software, lab dyeing machines

items.label: Common starting titles
items.value: Lab dip executive, colour matching trainee, dyeing lab assistant

items.label: Textile sector direct employment
items.note: Whole textile and apparel sector; an estimate, not tracked year by year

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Processing mills and dye makers hire textile-chemistry graduates as lab trainees. A good eye for colour (no colour-vision deficiency), lab practice in dyeing and finishing, and knowledge of dye classes help at interviews.

value.title: At a glance
items: Normal colour vision is usually tested.
Common next steps: senior colourist, dyeing lab head, or technical service with dye makers.
Often based at mills in textile clusters.

competition.note: B.Tech / B.E. (all branches) graduates in 2023-24 at institutions that reported to AISHE — everyone finishing that degree, not only those entering this role.
competition.source: AISHE 2023-24, Table 34 (programme-wise out-turn), Ministry of Education
